The winner played at most $\lceil\log_2 20\rceil=5$ matches, so 5 elements lost to it directly, and the maximum of those 5 needs 4 more comparisons. The total is $19+4=23=20+5-2$. The value 38 tempts because it is $2n-2$, the cost of two full scans.

lesson.summary: The maximum or minimum needs $n-1$ comparisons, both together $\lceil 3n/2\rceil-2$, and the second largest $n+\lceil\log_2 n\rceil-2$.

formulas.name: Big-O definition
formulas.tex: f(n) = O(g(n)) \iff \exists\, c > 0,\ n_0:\ 0 \le f(n) \le c\,g(n)\ \ \forall n \ge n_0
formulas.text: f(n) = O(g(n)) iff there exist c > 0 and n₀ with 0 ≤ f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀
formulas.note: Ω flips the inequality; Θ needs both with constants c₁ ≤ c₂.

formulas.name: Limit test for growth rates
formulas.tex: L = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{f(n)}{g(n)}:\quad L = 0 \Rightarrow f = o(g),\quad 0 < L < \infty \Rightarrow f = \Theta(g),\quad L = \infty \Rightarrow f = \omega(g)
formulas.text: L = lim f/g: L = 0 gives f = o(g); 0 < L < ∞ gives f = Θ(g); L = ∞ gives f = ω(g)
formulas.note: If the limit does not exist (f oscillating, such as n^(1 + sin n)), the test says nothing; use the definitions.

formulas.name: Stirling's estimate of log n!
formulas.tex: \log_2 n! = n\log_2 n - n\log_2 e + \Theta(\log n) = \Theta(n \log n)
formulas.text: log₂ n! = n log₂ n − n log₂ e + Θ(log n) = Θ(n log n)

formulas.name: Master theorem
formulas.tex: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n):\ \ T(n) = \begin{cases} \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) & f = O(n^{\log_b a - \varepsilon}) \\ \Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log^{k+1} n) & f = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log^k n),\ k \ge 0 \\ \Theta(f(n)) & f = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \varepsilon}),\ a f(n/b) \le c f(n),\ c < 1 \end{cases}
formulas.text: T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n): case 1 Θ(n^(log_b a)); case 2 Θ(n^(log_b a)·log^(k+1) n); case 3 Θ(f(n)) with regularity
where: a positive constant: the polynomial gap
formulas.note: Case 3 also needs the regularity condition; the polynomial gap ε is needed in cases 1 and 3, so n/log n against n is not case 1.

formulas.name: Recursion-tree total
formulas.text: T(n) = Σ (i = 0 to log_b n − 1) aⁱ·f(n/bⁱ) + Θ(n^(log_b a))
formulas.note: The leaf count a^(log_b n) equals n^(log_b a); a decreasing geometric series is dominated by its first term, an increasing one by its last.

formulas.name: Subtract-and-conquer expansions
formulas.text: T(n) = T(n − 1) + n gives n(n + 1)/2; T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 with T(0) = 1 gives 2^(n+1) − 1
formulas.note: With T(0) = 0 the second recurrence gives 2ⁿ − 1, the Towers of Hanoi move count; read the base case before writing an exact value.

formulas.name: Akra–Bazzi
formulas.text: Σ aᵢ·bᵢ^p = 1 gives T(n) = Θ(n^p·(1 + ∫₁ⁿ f(u)/u^(p+1) du))
where: coefficient of the i-th recursive call, aᵢ > 0
fraction of n passed to it, 0 < bᵢ < 1
formulas.note: Applies only to calls on constant fractions bᵢ·n; T(√n) is not of this form and needs a change of variable.

formulas.name: Doubling outer loop with inner loop to i
formulas.note: Equality 2n − 1 holds when n is a power of 2: n = 64 gives 127.

formulas.name: Harmonic sum
formulas.text: Σ (i = 1 to n) n/i = n·Hₙ = Θ(n log n)

formulas.name: Binary search worst-case probes
formulas.note: Counts loop iterations (middle elements examined). ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 agrees only when n is a power of 2: n = 1000 gives 10, not 11.

formulas.name: Comparison-sort lower bound
formulas.note: n = 5 gives ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7, and 7 comparisons do suffice for 5 elements.

formulas.name: Merge sort comparisons for n = 2ᵏ
formulas.tex: C_{\text{worst}} = n\log_2 n - n + 1,\qquad C_{\text{best}} = \tfrac{n}{2}\log_2 n
formulas.text: C_worst = n log₂ n − n + 1; C_best = (n/2)·log₂ n
formulas.note: One merge of sizes m and k costs at most m + k − 1 comparisons; summing over levels gives the worst case.

formulas.name: Build-heap cost
formulas.text: Σ ⌈n/2^(h+1)⌉·O(h) = O(n·Σ h/2ʰ) = O(n), since Σ h/2ʰ = 2

formulas.name: Insertion sort and inversions
formulas.text: T(n) = Θ(n + I), with 0 ≤ I ≤ n(n − 1)/2
where: number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]
formulas.note: The number of shifts equals I exactly; the number of comparisons lies between I and I + n − 1.

formulas.name: Counting and radix sort time
formulas.text: T_count = Θ(n + k); T_radix = Θ(d·(n + k))

formulas.name: Simultaneous minimum and maximum
formulas.note: Second largest instead needs n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2 comparisons.

complexity.name: Linear search
complexity.notes: Works on unsorted data and linked lists.

complexity.name: Interpolation search
complexity.notes: Average holds for uniformly distributed keys.

complexity.name: Selection sort
complexity.notes: Unstable, in-place, at most n − 1 swaps.

complexity.name: Quick sort
complexity.space: O(log n) average stack, O(n) worst
complexity.notes: Unstable, in-place; worst case on sorted input with an end pivot.

complexity.name: Heap sort
complexity.best: Θ(n log n) on distinct keys
complexity.notes: Unstable, in-place, not adaptive. With all keys equal every sift-down stops at once and the sort makes only Θ(n) comparisons.

complexity.name: Build-heap (bottom-up)
complexity.notes: Inserting the n keys one at a time costs Θ(n log n) worst case instead.

complexity.name: Radix sort (d digits, base k)
complexity.notes: Stable digit passes, least significant first.

complexity.name: Bucket sort (uniform keys)
complexity.notes: Worst case when every key falls in one bucket.

problemTypes.title: Solve a divide-and-conquer recurrence
recipe: Read off a, b and f(n), and compute c* = log_b a.
Compare f(n) with n^c*: polynomially smaller is case 1, equal up to logᵏ n is case 2, polynomially larger is case 3.
In case 2 multiply by one more log; in case 3 check a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) with c < 1 before answering Θ(f(n)).
If the form is T(n − 1) or T(√n), switch to expansion or a change of variable.
problemTypes.trap: Calling 2T(n/2) + n log n case 3 because n log n exceeds n: the excess is only a log factor, so it is case 2 with k = 1 and the answer is Θ(n log² n).

problemTypes.title: Order functions by growth or test an asymptotic statement
recipe: Place each function on the hierarchy: logs, then polynomials, then exponentials, then factorials.
For two functions in the same band, take logarithms or compute lim f/g.
Watch constants in exponents: 2ⁿ⁺¹ = Θ(2ⁿ) but 2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ.
problemTypes.trap: Treating n^(log n) as polynomial: its log is (log n)², so it outgrows every polynomial yet loses to 2^√n.

problemTypes.title: Count how often a statement in nested loops executes
recipe: Write the outer loop's values explicitly (1, 2, 4, … for doubling).
For each outer value, count the inner iterations as a function of it.
Sum the series: arithmetic, geometric or harmonic, and check with n = 4 or 8 by hand.
problemTypes.trap: Multiplying log n outer iterations by n inner iterations when the inner bound is i, not n: the geometric sum gives 2n − 1.

problemTypes.title: Best, worst, stability and in-place facts of a sort
recipe: Recall the master table row for each sort named.
For stability, ask whether an element can jump past an equal key: long-distance swaps (selection, quick, heap) break it.
For a special input (sorted, reversed, all equal), trace the pivot or the inner loop on n = 4.
problemTypes.trap: Assuming random-pivot quick sort has an O(n log n) worst case: only its expected time is n log n.

problemTypes.title: Exact number of comparisons
recipe: Identify the counted operation and the case (worst, best).
Use the matching count: ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 for binary search, n log₂ n − n + 1 for merge sort, ⌈log₂ n!⌉ for the decision-tree bound, ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 for min and max.
Sanity-check the formula on a tiny n by hand.
problemTypes.trap: Dropping the +1 in n log₂ n − n + 1, or writing ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 for binary search when n is not a power of 2.

problemTypes.title: Trace one pass of a sort or a heap build
recipe: Write the array with indices and follow the exact pseudocode the question gives.
For Lomuto, track i and swap on every a[j] ≤ pivot; for build-heap, sift down from index ⌊n/2⌋ − 1 to 0, continuing each sift until the node settles.
Compare the final array with each option position by position.
problemTypes.trap: Stopping a sift-down after one swap: the moved element may need to sink further, as 3 does when the root of [3, 6, 9, …] is fixed.

problemTypes.title: Pick the asymptotically best method for given data
recipe: Check the key type and range: small integer ranges allow counting or radix sort in Θ(n).
Check the input shape: nearly sorted favours insertion sort; a linked list favours merge sort.
Check constraints: stability needs merge or counting; O(1) space with guaranteed n log n needs heap sort.
problemTypes.trap: Answering Θ(n log n) for integers from a constant range: counting sort makes it Θ(n).

questions.stem: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n with T(1) = 1 has which solution?
questions.explanation: a = 2, b = 2, so c* = log₂ 2 = 1 and n^c* = n. f(n) = n log n = Θ(n¹ · log¹ n), which is master-theorem case 2 with k = 1, giving Θ(n log² n). It is not case 3: n log n exceeds n only by a log factor, not by a polynomial n^ε. Equivalently, each of the log₂ n levels costs about n·log(n/2ⁱ), and those sum to Θ(n log² n).

questions.stem: Solve T(n) = √n · T(√n) + n for n > 2, with T(2) = 1.
questions.explanation: Divide by n: T(n)/n = T(√n)/√n + 1. With S(n) = T(n)/n this is S(n) = S(√n) + 1. Taking square roots repeatedly, n = 2^(2ᵏ) reaches 2 after k = log₂ log₂ n steps, so S(n) = Θ(log log n) and T(n) = Θ(n log log n). The master theorem and Akra–Bazzi do not apply because the subproblem size √n is not a constant fraction of n.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements are true?
questions.explanation: 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·2ⁿ, a constant multiple, so it is O(2ⁿ). 2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ and 4ⁿ/2ⁿ = 2ⁿ → ∞, so it is not O(2ⁿ). Stirling gives log(n!) = n log n − Θ(n), which is Θ(n log n). n^(log₂ n) = 2^((log₂ n)²), and (log₂ n)² eventually exceeds 100 log₂ n, so it outgrows every fixed polynomial.

The outer loop takes i = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 (seven values). For each, the inner loop runs i times, so the total is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 64 = 2⁷ − 1 = 127. In general the total is 2n − 1 for n a power of 2, which is Θ(n), not Θ(n log n).

questions.stem: Iterative binary search (lo ≤ hi, mid = ⌊(lo + hi)/2⌋, one three-way comparison per iteration) runs on a sorted array of 1000 distinct elements. What is the maximum number of loop iterations over all search keys, present or absent?
questions.explanation: Each iteration roughly halves the live range, and the worst case takes ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 iterations. log₂ 1000 ≈ 9.97, so the answer is 9 + 1 = 10. Check: 10 iterations can distinguish up to 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1023 positions, and 9 can handle only 511 < 1000. Writing ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1 would give 11, which is wrong for n that is not a power of 2.

questions.stem: A sorted array of n integers may contain duplicates. What is the best worst-case time to count how many times a given value x occurs?
questions.explanation: Two binary searches find the first index with a[i] ≥ x and the first index with a[i] > x; their difference is the count. Each takes Θ(log n). Finding one copy of x and then scanning outward is Θ(n) when most of the array equals x.

questions.stem: Which of the following sorting algorithms, in their standard textbook form, are stable?
questions.explanation: Insertion sort shifts an element left only past strictly larger keys, and merge sort takes from the left half on ties, so both keep equal keys in input order. Heap sort's root-to-end swaps and quick sort's partition swaps can move an element past an equal one: quick sort on [2a, 2b, 1] with pivot 1 swaps 2a to the end, giving [1, 2b, 2a].

questions.stem: Insertion sort (shift larger elements right, then drop the key into the gap) sorts the array [4, 3, 2, 10, 12, 1, 5, 6] into ascending order. How many element shifts (assignments a[j + 1] = a[j]) are performed in total?
questions.explanation: Each shift fixes exactly one inversion, so the number of shifts equals the number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]. Counting per element against everything to its right: 4 > 3, 2, 1 gives 3; 3 > 2, 1 gives 2; 2 > 1 gives 1; 10 > 1, 5, 6 gives 3; 12 > 1, 5, 6 gives 3; 1, 5 and 6 give 0. Total = 3 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 3 = 12.

questions.stem: Top-down merge sort splits 8 elements into halves until single elements remain, then merges. What is the maximum number of key comparisons it can make over all inputs of 8 distinct keys?
questions.explanation: A merge of sizes m and k makes at most m + k − 1 comparisons. Level 1: four merges of 1 + 1, 1 each, so 4. Level 2: two merges of 2 + 2, 3 each, so 6. Level 3: one merge of 4 + 4, 7. Total 4 + 6 + 7 = 17, matching n log₂ n − n + 1 = 24 − 8 + 1. Every merge can hit its maximum at once, so 17 is reached.

questions.stem: Quick sort uses Lomuto partitioning: the pivot is the last element, and every a[j] ≤ pivot is swapped into the left block. On n keys, which inputs make it perform Θ(n²) comparisons?
options: A uniformly random permutation of distinct keys (expected count)
questions.explanation: Ascending: the pivot is the maximum, so the split is n − 1 and 0 every time, giving n(n − 1)/2 comparisons. Descending: the first pivot is the minimum, the swap leaves the maximum last, and the splits stay n − 1 against 0 at every level, again n(n − 1)/2. All equal: every key passes the ≤ test, so the pivot lands at the right end and the split is n − 1 against 0. A random permutation gives expected Θ(n log n), about 2n ln n comparisons.

questions.stem: Quick sort is modified so that each partition uses as pivot the exact median of the subarray, found by a worst-case Θ(n) selection algorithm. What is the worst-case running time on n elements?
questions.explanation: Selection and partition each cost Θ(n), and the median pivot splits the array into two halves of size about n/2, so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Θ(n) = Θ(n log n) for every input. No algorithm can do better, since any comparison sort needs Ω(n log n).

questions.stem: Bottom-up build-max-heap (sift down each node from index ⌊n/2⌋ − 1 down to 0, 0-indexed) is run on [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]. What is the resulting array?
questions.explanation: Index 3 (1) swaps with child 6: [3, 1, 4, 6, 5, 9, 2, 1]. Index 2 (4) swaps with 9: [3, 1, 9, 6, 5, 4, 2, 1]. Index 1 (1) swaps with the larger child 6, then stops against the equal child 1: [3, 6, 9, 1, 5, 4, 2, 1]. Index 0 (3) swaps with 9, landing at index 2, then swaps with its larger child 4: [9, 6, 4, 1, 5, 3, 2, 1]. Option B stops the last sift-down one swap early.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time to build a binary max-heap from an unordered array of n elements using bottom-up heapify?
questions.explanation: About n/2ʰ⁺¹ nodes sit at height h and each sift-down costs O(h), so the total is O(n·Σ h/2ʰ) = O(2n) = O(n); reading every element makes it Ω(n). Θ(n log n) is the cost of n successive inserts, not of bottom-up heapify.

questions.stem: What is the smallest asymptotic worst-case time to sort n integers, each in the range 1 to 100?
questions.explanation: Counting sort with k = 100 runs in Θ(n + 100) = Θ(n), and every element must be read, so Θ(n) is optimal. The Ω(n log n) bound applies only to sorts that learn the order by comparisons.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of comparisons that any comparison-based algorithm needs in the worst case to sort 5 distinct elements?
questions.explanation: The decision tree must have at least 5! = 120 leaves, so its height is at least ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7, since 2⁶ = 64 < 120 ≤ 128 = 2⁷. Merge insertion sorts 5 elements in 7 comparisons, so the bound is tight.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of comparisons needed in the worst case to find both the minimum and the maximum of 100 distinct numbers?
questions.explanation: Compare the elements in 50 pairs (50 comparisons). The 50 smaller ones compete for the minimum (49 comparisons) and the 50 larger ones for the maximum (49 comparisons). Total 50 + 49 + 49 = 148 = ⌈3·100/2⌉ − 2. Two separate scans would use 99 + 98 = 197.

pitfalls.text: f = O(n²) is only an upper bound: n = O(n²) is true. When a question asks for the tight order, answer with Θ.
The master theorem needs a polynomial gap in cases 1 and 3. A log-factor difference such as n log n against n is case 2 with k = 1, not case 3.
Case 3 also needs the regularity condition a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) with c < 1; it holds for polynomials but must be checked for oscillating f.
Build-heap is Θ(n), not Θ(n log n); heap sort as a whole is still Θ(n log n) because of the n − 1 extractions.
Random or median-of-three pivots improve the expected time only; quick sort's worst case stays Θ(n²) unless the pivot is the exact median.
Selection sort is Θ(n²) even on sorted input, while insertion and early-exit bubble sort are Θ(n) there.
Stable and in-place are independent properties: merge sort is stable but not in-place, heap sort is in-place but not stable.
Counting sort is linear only when the key range k is O(n); for keys up to n² it costs Θ(n²) time and space.

errata.claim: n^(1/log n) is a constant equal to e.
errata.correction: n^(1/log_b n) = b, the base of the logarithm. It equals e only for the natural log; with log₂, the usual convention in algorithm analysis, it equals 2. It is Θ(1) in every case.

errata.claim: PYQ-7 and practice Q12: the maximum number of binary-search comparisons on n elements is ⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1, giving 11 for n = 1024.
errata.correction: The worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, as section 8.3 states. The two agree for n = 1024 (both give 11), but the ceiling form is wrong whenever n is not a power of 2: for n = 1000 the maximum is 10, not 11.

errata.claim: PYQ-8: T(n) = √n·T(√n) + n is solved by Akra–Bazzi or expansion.
errata.correction: Akra–Bazzi does not apply, because it requires subproblems of size bᵢ·n for constants bᵢ < 1, and √n is not of that form. Divide by n and set S(n) = T(n)/n to get S(n) = S(√n) + 1, so T(n) = Θ(n log log n).
The version given (count array plus a separate output array) uses Θ(n + k) extra space, as section 17.1 states. Only the count array is Θ(k).
